extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary theory, poets/playwrights, and scholars of classical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and reading drama derived from Aristotle's Poetics and its introductory commentary — emphasizing plot, naturalness, and emotional appeal rather than purely intellectual argument. Useful for writers, critics, and students of classical literary theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot / Story as the core of drama
rubrics_metrics.description: "He reduces the drama to its language, people say, and the language itself to its least poetic element, the story" — the Poetics treats story (plot) as central to drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drama primarily by its plot: the sequence of actions and events is the foundational element. Beware of oversimplifying tragedy into moralistic Aesop-like fables; the plot should have appropriate complexity and avoid childish reduction. (Context: the introduction notes critics' charge that Aristotle reduces drama to story, and defends the centrality of plot.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to the heart as well as the intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: "Aristotle criticizes orators who write exclusively from the intellect, rather than from the heart, in the way Sophocles makes Antigone speak."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good rhetorical/poetic practice engages emotion ('the heart') not only cold reason. When evaluating or composing drama, prioritize passages and arguments that move readers/audiences emotionally and feel authentic, rather than those that are merely clever or purely intellectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor naturalness/appropriateness (phusikôs) over mere logicalness (logikôs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle "regularly uses the adverb logikôs, logically, as a term of reproach contrasted with phusikôs, naturally or appropriately, to describe arguments made by others, or preliminary and inadequate arguments of his own."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess elements (plot developments, character actions, rhetorical moves, language) for how 'natural' or 'appropriate' they are to the work, rather than whether they are strictly logical in an abstract sense. 'Logically' constructed parts that feel forced or preliminary may be inferior to those that arise organically from the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from canonical models and close reading
rubrics_metrics.description: "Aristotle himself respected Homer so much that he personally corrected a copy of the Iliad... Those who take the trouble to look at the Poetics closely will find... reflections of a good reader and characteristically powerful thinker."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful, attentive reading of great works (e.g., Homer, Sophocles) as part of forming and judging dramatic practice. Respect for tradition and detailed textual attention are presented as part of becoming a knowledgeable critic or practitioner; look for the substantive reflections and guidance contained within close study of the Poetics.
